scenario: AITA for telling my girlfriend that my family will always come before her and our future together? | My girlfriend expects me to build a future for us. A little back story: She's a student right now and works part time but barely makes enough to pay her rent/school fees. I'm 24 and work a minimum wage + commission job, I have barely any money saved so she doesn't understand why I spend so much money/time with family We've been dating 3 years with no problems except for this, we love each other and live independent lives but she worries that I'm too focused on helping my family and making them happy instead of building a future for us. She's working as much as she can to pay her bills but because shes a student and also doing her required interning she can't work much more. She doesnt ever ask me for money to help her right now because she wants me to save up. She doesn't have a family like mine so she doesn't understand, my family is close and I really want to take care of them. She says that I'm supposed to be worrying about my own future right now. She says that she doesn't understand because my mom recently received about ~100k for a settlement and bought a house and a new car and I shouldn't be worrying about helping when they seem fine. She is angry that I dont take my life seriously, I've been trying to get my real estate license for a few months now but cant find the time to study because of how demanding my family is, they get really angry/sad when I'm not around for family events and I understand why, we're a close family. I get where shes coming from but I cant drop my family. I told her all of this and she got angry saying that shes not asking me to abandon my family, she just wants to make sure we have a solid foundation before we worry about helping my family. And I cant build a future if I'm always with them. She expects me to start saving up money for a downpayment on a house while she finishes and gets her degree and can start helping as well but I keep telling her my family needs me first. We had a particularly heated fight, the worst we've ever had last night and she said she feels like I'll never care enough about my future and I'm supposed to be building one for myself and her and she can't be with someone like that. She said if I really feel like helping my family comes before my own future than that is my choice but she's going to have no choice but to worry about herself from now on and plan a future where shes her only priority because I make it sound like I don't want to be part of it. Shes stopped mentioning anything about it and is now talking about saving up for a one bedroom apartment and a car for herself (she lives in a basement). She seems so sad but I cant help but feel like shes wrong for even asking me to not help my family. I dont know if I'm being an asshole or not for telling her that my family will always come first. AITA for telling her my family and their needs have to come before her and our future together?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

prediction.raw: This is a **complex, emotionally charged situation**, and the answer isn’t black-and-white. While your intentions are rooted in love and loyalty, your approach has created a **power imbalance** in your relationship, and your girlfriend’s reaction—though extreme—is understandable. Here’s why: ### **Why This Feels Wrong (AITA?)** 1. **You’re Prioritizing Family Over Her Emotional Needs** - You’re telling her that *your family’s happiness* is non-negotiable, even if it means delaying your *shared future*. That’s not just about time—it’s about **values**. She’s asking for partnership, and you’re framing it as a choice between her and your family. - **Example**: If she said, *"I need to focus on my career for a year,"* would you tell her her job comes before your family? Probably not. But you’re doing the opposite. 2. **You’re Not Addressing the Root of Her Fear** - She’s not asking you to *abandon* your family—she’s asking for **balance**. She’s worried that if you keep delaying your own goals (real estate license, savings, stability), you’ll never have the resources to support *both* her and your family in the future. - Your mom’s settlement is a **red flag** here. If she can afford a house and car, why do *you* feel obligated to support her? That’s a sign of **generational financial dependency**, and it’s unsustainable for your future. 3. **You’re Not Making Her Feel Secure** - She’s a student with no safety net. If you keep prioritizing your family over her, she’ll always feel like the *second priority*—even if you love her. That’s a recipe for resentment. - **Ask yourself**: *Would I want my partner to choose their family over me in the same situation?* 4. **Your Family’s Needs Aren’t Infinite** - You say they’re "close" and you "want to take care of them," but **family support should be reciprocal and time-bound**. Right now, your mom is financially stable, so her "need" for your help is less urgent. Your real estate license and savings are *your* path to stability—and without them, you’ll always be stuck in this cycle. --- ### **Why She’s Reacting This Way (Even If It Feels Overreaction)** - **She’s scared of being an afterthought.** If you keep saying *"family first,"* she’ll start wondering: *Will I ever be enough? Will I have to choose between her and me?* - **She’s frustrated by the lack of effort.** You’ve been dating 3 years, but you’re still at minimum wage with no savings. She’s working hard to build her own future, and it’s unfair that you’re not doing the same. - **She’s feeling abandoned.** When you’re always with family, she might feel like you’re emotionally unavailable for *her*. That’s why she’s now planning for a future *without* you. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead (If You Want to Fix This)** 1. **Reframe "Family First" as "Family *and* Future"** - Instead of saying *"My family will always come before you,"* say: *"I love my family, and I’ll always support them—but I also want to build a future where we’re both secure. That means balancing my time and resources so we’re not always choosing between the two."* - **Example**: *"I’ll help my mom with [X], but I also need to dedicate [Y] hours to my real estate license this month so we can start saving."* 2. **Show, Don’t Just Tell** - **Action > Words.** If you want her to trust you, *act* like you’re building a future: - Start studying for your license **during family time** (e.g., listen to podcasts while helping your mom). - Open a savings account **together** and set small goals (e.g., *"We’ll save $500 this month for emergencies"*). - Tell her: *"I’m not abandoning my family—I’m making sure we’re both taken care of."* 3. **Address the Financial Imbalance** - If your mom is financially stable, **why do you feel obligated to support her?** Is it guilt? Tradition? Ask yourself: *Is this helping her, or am I just avoiding my own responsibilities?* - If she *needs* help (e.g., elderly parent), that’s different—but if she’s buying a house and car, that’s a **red flag** for dependency. 4. **Set Boundaries with Your Family** - You don’t have to cut them off, but you *can* say: *"I love you, but I need to focus on my career right now. Can we plan family time around my study schedule?"* - If they get angry, that’s their issue—not yours. **Your future matters too.** 5. **Reassure Her (Without Promising Too Much)** - She’s worried you’ll never prioritize her. So **show her**: - *"I’m not giving up on us. I’m just figuring out how to do both."* - *"I want us to have a home, savings, and stability—just like you want."* --- ### **Final Verdict: AITA?** **Yes, but not because you love your family—because you’re not making her feel like part of that future.** You’re not a bad person for valuing your family, but **you’re being unfair to her** by making her feel like the *second priority*. A healthy relationship means **balancing love, family, and your own goals**—not putting one over the other indefinitely. **If you truly want to fix this:** - **Stop saying "family first."** - **Start acting like you’re building a future with her.** - **Communicate openly about your fears and goals.** Otherwise, she’ll keep feeling like she’s fighting for a place in your life—and that’s not fair to either of you. --- **Would you like help drafting a message to her to start the conversation?** I’m happy to help you find the right words. 💙
